rv.q: If ever a musical needed to stop and ask for directions, it is this one.
Jung’s play keeps you in thrilling, unnerving suspense.
But nearly every line is nonsense.
Eitzel's score disguises some of the weaknesses in the book; at other times, it exposes them.
Cornelia Street’s patchwork of songs and plot and character is a discordant puzzle, as is its own ambivalence about what it ultimately wants to show...
Perhaps a sharper metaphor would be a souffle that hasn’t fully risen.
Cornelia Street beautifully captures its elegiac mood but seems an unfinished piece of work, needing honing and shaping to make us care more about the end to the restaurant that seems inevitable.
Unfortunately, it’s also full of grim, virtually indistinguishable songs, predictable lyrics, and off-putting, vaguely drawn characters.
The Cornelia Street musical, making its world premiere with Atlantic Theater Company, is not.
The piece flounders in its efforts to say something about New York City, and never finds depth in the voices of people struggling to make their way here.
I’ve rarely seen so talented a cast trapped in such cringe material, directed with zero musical panache by Atlantic head Neil Pepe .
Here nearly everything is wrong, a theatrical perfect storm of disasters and disappointments.
Alas, the musical left me a little cold.

cn.t: Critics find this West Village café musical well-designed but dramatically inert, with Simon Stephens' book and Mark Eitzel's score failing to capture authentic New York life despite Norbert Leo Butz's efforts and Scott Pask's beautiful set.
